title: Resonance, Rhythm and Coherence
reflection: Choose one rhythm to keep steady this week, such as a bedtime or six slow breaths, and one person or place that settles you.

questions.q: What is resonance, according to Conversation 3.6?
o: Matching a rhythm so that a tiny input moves a great deal, like pushing a swing at the right moment.
Repeating a rhythm for as long as possible, so that the body grows tired and gives way.
Blocking out every rhythm but one, so that the mind is left quiet and undisturbed.
Raising the volume of a signal, so that it can be heard above all of the surrounding noise.
questions.e: Small pushes at exactly the right moment build a huge arc. Your mind is always resonating with something: a calm presence settles you and an agitated one unsettles you, often without a word.
questions.c: Resonance: match the rhythm and a small input moves a great deal

questions.q: A man says he will avoid resonating with anything, to stay calm. What does Conversation 3.6 reply?
o: You cannot switch resonance off, but you can choose what you place yourself near.
He can switch it off by practice, if only he is willing to keep at it long enough.
He should resonate with everything equally, so that no single thing has any hold.
He should resonate with nothing but his own thoughts, since they are the safest.
questions.e: You cannot switch resonance off. Practice makes you a finely tuned fork, responsive to what is true and unmoved by the trivial, and not a loose string buzzing at everything.
questions.c: You cannot switch resonance off, only choose what is near

questions.q: A woman’s sleep and meals are erratic, and she feels frayed. What does Conversation 3.6 suggest?
o: Rhythm is medicine: steady time stabilises everything, and routine is a floor for finer practice.
Rhythm does not matter much, since the mind is quite free of the body and of its clock.
Rhythm is only for young children, since an adult can run on any pattern that happens to suit.
Rhythm is a luxury, to be added only once every other part of life has been fully settled.
questions.e: The body is built to run in rhythm, and fighting it carries a real cost. About six slow breaths a minute shifts the body toward calm in minutes. Routine is the stable floor every finer practice stands on.
questions.c: Rhythm is medicine; routine is the floor

questions.q: “Tamas is a heavy slowness that looks like rest but is really stuckness.”
questions.e: The lesson names the three guṇas as three rhythms: sattva a steady harmonious beat, rajas a fast erratic over-activity, and tamas a collapsed heavy slowness that looks like rest but is stuckness.
questions.c: Tamas looks like rest but is stuckness

questions.q: What does the bulb and laser picture show, in Conversation 3.6?
o: The same energy can scatter or line up and cut steel: coherence is being in step.
A bulb is better than a laser, since a gentle glow is easier on the eyes of everyone.
A laser needs far more energy than a bulb, so only a strong person can be coherent.
A bulb and a laser are two names for one thing, which light can show in either way.
questions.e: A bulb scatters light for a modest glow; a laser lines every wave up and cuts steel. When thought, feeling and action scatter you work hard and light little; when they line up, the inner fighting stops and energy stops leaking.

questions.q: A teacher thinks one thing, feels another and does a third, and ends each day exhausted. Which idea fits Conversation 3.6?
o: Scattered thought, feeling and action leak energy; lining them up is sattva.
Exhaustion is the sign of a hard job, so the only thing to do is to work still harder.
The three are meant to differ, so she should learn to keep them well apart in the day.
Exhaustion comes from her body alone, so a longer sleep is the whole of the remedy.
questions.e: When thought, feeling and action line up, the inner fighting stops and you feel powerful even at hard tasks. That aligned state is sattva. The coherent mind also sees more truly, since the flicker between your version and reality slows.
questions.c: Line up thought, word and deed

questions.q: A man notices that his breath and body settle when he sits with a steady friend. What does Conversation 3.6 call this?
o: Entrainment: two nervous systems fall into step, which is why wise company is a real support.
Imagination: he is picturing the calm, so no real change has taken place in him.
A weakness: he depends on others, so he should learn to settle on his own alone.
Chance: the friend’s mood has no effect, so it only happens to coincide with his own.
questions.e: Put two nervous systems near each other and they tend to fall into step. This is why wise company, satsaṅga, was treated as a real support and not a luxury.
questions.c: Wise company is a real support: we catch each other’s rhythm

questions.q: “A group that chants and moves together locks into one field, and the field amplifies whatever is in it, so discernment must walk alongside.”
questions.e: The lesson gives the Ṛgveda’s recipe for tuning together. The field amplifies whatever is in it, which is why discernment is needed: a fearful crowd amplifies fear.
questions.c: The field amplifies what is in it, so discernment must walk alongside

questions.q: A woman wants to tune herself from the inside, without anyone else. What does Conversation 3.6 suggest?
o: Rehearse a feeling-tone such as warmth or steadiness each day, until her system rests there on its own.
Wait for a good mood to arrive, and then try to hold it for as long as she can.
Avoid all company, since every other person is certain to disturb her rhythm.
Think about calm all day, since the thought of calm is the same as the thing itself.
questions.e: This is bhāva, tuning from the inside: rehearse a feeling-tone daily until your system rests there. It works alongside the outer supports of rhythm and wise company.

questions.q: What does it mean to be a finely tuned fork rather than a loose string, in Conversation 3.6?
o: To be responsive to what is true and unmoved by the trivial, and not buzzing at everything.
To be very tense and watchful, so that nothing can ever slip past the notice of the mind.
To be still and silent at all times, so that nothing can set up a vibration at all.
To be sensitive to every sound, so that nothing can ever be missed by the person.
questions.e: Practice does not make you numb. It makes you responsive to what is true and unmoved by the trivial, a finely tuned fork and not a loose string buzzing at everything.
questions.c: A tuned fork answers what is true and ignores the trivial
